lesson.title: Who decides what’s fair?
lesson.subtitle: Five questions to ask of any AI

video.title: Who decides what’s fair?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — teacher educator from Bangladesh, visiting the school’s AI club (main character)
Mr Okafor — science teacher who runs the school’s AI club (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer, speaking to the student)

chapters.label: What you can do, and the lab

scenes.visual: The school’s AI club after lessons: chairs in a circle, ‘AI club’ written on the whiteboard. Dr Farah holds up a glossy leaflet showing a camera over a grid of simple face outlines, with the line ‘Register in seconds!’. Students lean in; one frowns, one looks impressed.
scenes.animation: Leaflet slides up into Dr Farah’s hand (200 ms); a small clock icon ticks once; push-in on the students’ faces.
scenes.narration: Your head teacher just showed me a camera that takes the register by recognising faces. It would save ten minutes a day. Should your school buy it?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: who decides what’s fair, and five questions to ask any AI.

scenes.visual: A clean white card. Five rows build one by one, each an icon with its question: scales (fair), a padlock (private), an eye (open), a person (responsible), a raised hand (agreed). The face camera from the hook sits small in a corner, being ‘tested’ by each question.
scenes.animation: Each row slides in as it is named, 250 ms apart; a soft tick on each icon.
scenes.narration: Five questions fit any AI. Is it fair: does it work for everyone? Is it private: what data, and who sees it? Is it open about how it decides? Who answers for its mistakes? And did the people it affects agree?

scenes.visual: The face camera points at two students in uniform. Split screen: on the left, a student at her desk gets a red ‘absent’ mark and a worried parent appears at home; on the right, an empty desk gets a green ‘present’ tick and nobody looks for the missing boy. A balance scale hangs between the two halves, unsure which way to tip.
scenes.animation: Left half wipes in, then the right; the scale wobbles, then stops level with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Behind every AI are people’s choices, like which mistake is worse. If the camera marks a present student absent, they may be in trouble at home. If it marks an absent one present, nobody notices they’re missing. Which is worse? People decide: it’s a value, not a fact.

scenes.visual: Three warning cards: a phone playing a voice note with a teacher’s face outline and a ‘fake’ stamp; a photo of a cartoon classmate being edited by a sparkle wand, with a hurt face nearby; a market street seen through camera frames that follow each shopper.
scenes.animation: Cards flip in one by one; the camera frames hop from shopper to shopper.
scenes.narration: Some harms come from how AI is used. Deepfakes are AI-made photos, voices or videos that look real, like a fake voice note from a teacher, or a picture made to hurt a classmate. And face recognition can track people through a market without them knowing.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. The words ‘Does it work?’ shrink to one side as ‘Is it right to use?’ grows in the centre. Below, three numbered questions build: who gains, who could be harmed, who gets a say.
scenes.animation: Text swap with a gentle scale (300 ms); steps appear 300 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: AI ethics: right, not just working
scenes.narration: So, AI ethics asks whether an AI is right to use, not just whether it works. It weighs who gains, who could be harmed, and who gets a say.

scenes.visual: A school notice board with a new rule pinned to it. Dr Farah stands beside it. Ticks appear next to ‘fair to everyone’, ‘explained to everyone’ and a name of who answers for it. Then a second rule appears inside a locked box nobody can open; students shrug. Finally the rule card turns into a small robot that pins itself to the board.
scenes.animation: Ticks pop (150 ms each); the locked box rattles once; the rule card morphs into the robot (400 ms).
scenes.narration: Think of a school rule. A good rule is fair, explained to everyone, and someone answers for it. A secret rule nobody can question feels wrong, even when it works. An AI that decides is a rule that runs itself.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor pops in beside the face camera and the balance scale from earlier, marker in hand. Three answer cards drop in below him.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Who should have a say in which mistake the camera treats as worse?

scenes.visual: The card ‘The school, students and their families’ gets a check badge. Groups appear around the camera: students and parents, the head teacher with staff, and builders at a laptop. A loop arrow shows a setting being changed after they talk.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the loop arrow draws itself (600 ms).
scenes.on_screen_text: People choose, so people can change
scenes.narration: The people it affects, as well as those who make and use it. Every AI carries choices about goals, data and trade-offs. Good news: choices can be questioned, and changed.

scenes.visual: A phone receives a shocking voice note in a class group. A hand hovers over ‘Forward’, stops, and instead taps ‘Call’ to the real teacher. Then: a crossed-out ‘make a fake’ button; a student talking to a trusted adult; a student raising a hand at an assembly to ask the five questions.
scenes.animation: Each action card slides in as it is said; the ‘Forward’ button greys out.
scenes.narration: What can you do? If a photo, voice note or video shocks you, check before sharing: ask the person in it, or find the source. Never make or forward a fake of a real person, even as a joke. Report fakes to an adult you trust. If someone wants to watch you with AI, ask the five questions.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the ‘Decide with numbers’ lab: four sliders (cost, learning, travel time, safety) and three bars for a museum, a farm and a science centre. A finger drags the ‘safety’ slider up; the leading bar changes.
scenes.animation: Slider thumb drags (600 ms); bars resize smoothly; the winning bar glows.
scenes.narration: In the app, choose a class trip: museum, farm or science centre. Set how much cost, learning, travel and safety matter, and watch the best choice change. The maths stays the same; the values are yours.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside the face camera, which now shows a perfect score: every face ticked. Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Imagine the camera recognises every student correctly. Does that settle whether your school should use it?

scenes.visual: The ‘No’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into a summary: the five question icons in a row, a balance scale held by people’s hands, and a phone with a ‘check first’ shield.
scenes.animation: Points tick in one by one; the takeaway bar rises last.
scenes.on_screen_text: Five questions · People’s choices · Check fakes
scenes.narration: No: accuracy answers just one of five questions. Remember: ask all five. An AI’s values are people’s choices, so they can be questioned. And check fakes before you share.

scenes.visual: A classroom (or a family round a table at home): two groups facing each other, a card reading ‘Face recognition for attendance?’ between them. Each side holds up question cards with the five icons. Hands go up for a vote. Dr Farah smiles at the side.
scenes.animation: Question cards flip up on each side; hands rise for the vote; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: hold a short debate at home or in class. Should our school use face recognition for attendance? Both sides use the five questions. Then vote, and say what would change your mind.

checkpoints.prompt: Who should have a say in which mistake the school camera treats as worse?

options.text: Only the company that built it
Nobody: the camera works it out
The school, students and their families

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — which mistake is worse is a value, not a fact, so the people it affects should have a say, as well as the school that uses it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — which mistake is worse is a value people choose, so the students and families it affects should have a say, not only the makers.

checkpoints.prompt: The camera recognises every student correctly. Does that settle whether your school should use it?

options.text: Yes — if it’s accurate, it’s fine
No — privacy and consent still matter

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — accuracy answers one question of five. Privacy, openness, responsibility and consent still need answers.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — even a perfectly accurate camera leaves the other questions: privacy, openness, who’s responsible and who agreed.
